<reason>B wins on the mandatory five-year deadline, not on the merits of universal subsidies. A convincingly explains regressivity and defeats B's claim that broad cash coverage necessarily eliminates savings. But A commits to withdrawal even if millions remain outside payments, without establishing why five years reliably resolves delivery failures. B's capacity-triggered alternative makes the stronger comparison between delayed reform and uncompensated losses. A's deadline-as-incentive argument does not outweigh that risk. B's overstated fiscal claims and clipped turns keep the victory competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's second pressure question exposes the conflict between guaranteed completion and compensation-first sequencing. A answers honestly but offers expanded eligibility rather than demonstrated payment delivery. B then persuasively argues that legal indexation and enrollment promises cannot themselves overcome the weak capacity motivating the objection.</best_rebuttal>
